feedback.body: How messy is it going to be to register/unregister message sources when entering/exiting from a given operating mode?

replies.author: turnrye
replies.body:
It wouldn't be that messy, but I'm not sure yet that it's what we'd want to do. Right now the registry already gates by the current mode. `messages_task(mode)` and `findSource(mode)` mean a source that isn't for the active mode is just inactive, so there's nothing to unregister on a switch. With a single source, registering once at init comes out identical to doing it per-opmode, so I've kept the simple version here.

Even with more protocols I'd lean toward leaving them registered rather than toggling on every mode enter/exit. My thought is, the sources are tiny and stateless. Why do more state transition etc than needed. 

The thing I do think deserves a cleanup by then is what you've flagged here; having each opmode own its registration (registered as it comes up) would read a lot cleaner than a stack of #ifs in the thread. I can do that now, or we can do it once APRS (and APRS-over-M17) get added.

replies.author: turnrye
replies.body:
Rather than register/unregister per mode, I kept the sources passthroughl. They don't keep any buffers of their own. M17 SMS just reads out of the packet on the way in and writes into the registry's buffer on the way out, so there's nothing per-source to allocate or free when the mode changes.

And the inbox storage only exists while a messaging mode is active, so sources don't stack up at startup. I think we should plan to hold APRS to the same bar and only add a shared buffer if it really needs one.

feedback.body:
Apart from code cleanliness, dynamic registration will allow each message source to allocate/release memory resources if needed. Now we do not need it, but in the future it may be the case, and it may happen that having multiple message sources being initialized at startup exhaust the RAM even if there is enough memory to run each of them individually. As usual, I tend towards future-proofing :smile: 

But if you say that is good enough :tm: for the time being, we can keep it as it is.

From what I remember an erased eMMC reads all zeroes instead of 0xFFFF. Actually the intent of my comment was to make the implementation future-proof rather than covering an existing case.

About the fill with 0xFF: I re-read all the code and now I understand why you do so. It came to my mind a case where this is not very efficient, though: when the NVM storage is an I2C eeprom (like in GD-77 and DM-1801) the settings system is filling an entire block with 0xFF and immediately after it writes a valid entry at the top. Apart from taking some time, this spends extra write life of the eeprom memory itself every time a block needs to be erased.

If I understood all the logic correctly, we can probably change it to consider a partition either "valid" or "invalid", with the latter case being either a partition with corrupted data or a totally empty one. When writing to an invalid partition, then, it will be enough to directly write the new data block (preceded by an erase, if necessary) without the 0xFF fill.
The only downside of this approach that comes to my mind is that, when an already-erased flash memory is used, this will be considered invalid and erased again even if not necessary. This, however, should happen only the first time the code is run on the device. 

What do you think? I could have missed some important detail...

feedback.body:
> I mainly renamed STM32Flash to internalFlash.

I'd have kept it named `stm32Flash`, so that there is a reference to the target device. Actually, I'd change the prefix of the function names to `flashStm32`: we already have `spiStm32` and `adcStm32` in the drivers, so I'd go on with this convention for consistency.

> I then moved the two copies of flash.h to peripherals/flash.h. I also added two variables to stm32yyyxxx/flash.c instead of internal_flash.c.

> There is a lot of common code for the logic of the internal flash itself, should it stay in the header file?

From the partial reorganization you did, I can see that in the end the common code is around 70 lines: I think we can just have it duplicated in the two implementation files and call it a day.

So, I'd go for a common header file and two different implementations for each MCU family. This allows also for some optimizations: for example in the case of the STM32H7 the function performing bounds checking on the address can be reduced to checking only if the address is above or below the address range.

> I had to remove the const specifier to some nvm structs and deciced to remove them all. I don't think it makes that much sense to keep them and it makes it impossible to have reasonably flexible code without massive code deduplication.

The NVM structs have to be `const` actually: the reason is that, by doing so, their instances end up in the `.rodata` area which resides in flash memory. Given that in the 99% of the cases the data contained in those structs will never change, is better to not "waste" RAM space for them.

You can have const pointers to structs and still be able to change their fields. I'm already doing this in the zephyr flash driver: https://github.com/OpenRTX/OpenRTX/blob/b262fd5fe1e1959c53f24d39cc08b8b8b9920941/platform/drivers/NVM/flash_zephyr.h#L29 https://github.com/OpenRTX/OpenRTX/blob/b262fd5fe1e1959c53f24d39cc08b8b8b9920941/platform/drivers/NVM/flash_zephyr.c#L32

To handle the additional information for the STM32F4 flash, I'd do the following:
```
#define INTERNAL_FLASH_DEVICE_DEFINE(name)        \
    static struct nvmInfo name##_nvmInfo;         \
    static struct internalFlashArea name##_priv;  \
    static struct nvmDevice name = {              \
        .priv = &name##_priv,                     \
        .ops = &internalFlash_ops,                \
        .info = &name##_nvmInfo,                  \
     };
```
and then fill the fields of `priv` in the initialization function.

Another option is to go back to the `enum` for sector sizes and have something like this:
```
enum sectorSize {
    SECTOR_SIZE_16K
    SECTOR_SIZE_64K
    SECTOR_SIZE_128K
};

#define INTERNAL_FLASH_DEVICE_DEFINE(name, sector_size)        \
    static struct nvmInfo name##_nvmInfo;         \
    static struct nvmDevice name = {              \
        .priv = (const void *) sector_size,                     \
        .ops = &internalFlash_ops,                \
        .info = &name##_nvmInfo,                  \
     };
```
and then use `dev->priv` as the index into the array of `struct internalFlashArea`. For STM32H7 this will be unused, but this detail is hidden into the implementation file.

I'd say, let's make the header file device-specific for STM32. We also have to take into account that other MCUs may have different ways to access and manage the internal flash memory, so we'll probably end up having a set of device-specific drivers in any case.
Another thing that I forgot to mention, is that I'd like to move all the drivers that can be directly instantiated from OpenRTX main codebase into the `platform/drivers` folder.

> Ok, let's step back and make sure of what to do. I have two PR waiting to be reviewed and I can't afford to rewrite each PR three times to change the angle of attack, change the features set, or handle hypothetical use cases.
> 
> This PR was initially mainly for Module17 to store settings using the current nvm driver. I thus created a driver for the internal flash of that MCU (that covers more than half the OpenRTX devices). I also added support for STM32H743 because this was a low-hanging fruit. Then I had to make the header device generic which is a major PITA because of all the const values everywhere in the storage driver. Now I need to make the header device specific and we are talking about supporting MCUs that, for now, don't need this driver.
> 
> I say, we fix minor issues about this driver and move on. Later down the road, if we need to support additional devices, we will see if it requires making the driver device specific. It will probably not because the header file contains basically nothing except for the type of driver and the sector size (which is generic enough).

Acyually in my mind the plan was to go just for an STM32F4-specific driver to minimize the effort, but I wasn't clear in telling that.
Sorry for the mess and thanks for the patience. ❤️

> Ok, only thing left:
> 
> Should we rewrite the MDx/Mod17 nvmem api to use this one? Those two devices are the only reason I left the original flash.h/flash.c files.

I'd say no. When the new setting system is deployed, we move everything to the new API and then cleanup all the old files
